A1-001: A class is the plan; an object is one instance made from that plan. Like Python's Car(), C++ can create many separate Car objects. A method belongs to a class, but is not itself the object.
A1-002: In the simplified exam model, live objects use working memory (RAM), not read-only ROM. Automatic objects and dynamically allocated objects have different storage durations. Real machines also use caches, and an optimizer can remove an unnecessary object; this question is not asking about those implementation details.
A1-003: The key selects D, but the wording confuses scope with lifetime. Scope tells where a name is visible; storage duration and initialization govern when its object exists. A data type determines representation, not by itself the moment of creation. Learn the distinction rather than treating all three as interchangeable.
A1-004: A constructor has the same name as its class and no return type: Car(). The parentheses hold parameters, if any. ~Car() is a destructor; neither -Car nor ()Car is constructor syntax.
A1-005: Use object.member for an object and pointer->member for a pointer. Thus A and B are both valid in their respective situations, and C summarizes them. With this paper's multiple-true convention, D is the intended answer.
A1-006: C++ has three access specifiers: public, protected and private. They control access to class members. Do not copy this count directly to Java, which also has package access when no modifier is written.
A1-007: You cannot directly instantiate an abstract class. A concrete derived class can be instantiated after it supplies the required final implementations. Pointers and references to an abstract base are still allowed.
A1-008: The key's answer 3 is a beginner classification: default, parameterized and copy. It is not an exhaustive C++ language rule: modern C++ also has move constructors and other useful categories. The question must specify its textbook classification before one numerical answer is defensible.
A1-009: The usual introductory split is compile-time and runtime polymorphism. Overloading is selected from the declared argument types; a virtual call can select an override using the object's runtime type. This two-category teaching model is what the question asks.
A1-010: Inheritance creates the base/derived relationship: Car is a Vehicle. Encapsulation groups and protects state; polymorphism lets the same operation behave differently. Those ideas can work together, but the relationship itself is inheritance.
A1-011: Public is often a useful interface design, which explains key A, but a C++ virtual function may legally be public, protected or private. Access and overriding are separate rules. Because 'should' does not state a design requirement, this is discussion rather than a uniquely graded fact.
A1-012: A virtual operation is introduced in a base class, but its implementation may be in that base, in derived classes, or both. A pure virtual declaration need not have an ordinary base implementation. 'Defined' is not the same as 'first declared', so key B is not a universal answer.
A1-013: One try block can have multiple catch handlers, each for a different kind of exception. Put specific handlers before general ones. Only the first matching handler handles a particular thrown exception.
A1-014: The two-colon token :: is scope resolution. Car::start names a class member; std::cout names a namespace member; ::x can select a global variable hidden by a local x. A single colon and ?: have different jobs.
A1-015: std::cout is a standard output stream object. The << token is the insertion operator used with it. The pair std::cout << 5 sends the value 5 to standard output; cout is not itself the operator.
A1-016: A constructor has no return type, not even void. Calling a constructor initializes an object; this does not make the constructor an ordinary function returning a class value. Write Car(), not void Car().
A1-017: The simple textbook example has zero parameters, which is key A. The precise C++ rule is that a default constructor can be called with zero arguments. Car(int x = 0) also qualifies although it has one parameter. The question incorrectly treats parameters and required arguments as the same thing.
A1-018: Single-level inheritance describes the shape of a class relationship, not 'runtime inheritance'. A derived class directly inherits from one base in the usual example. Runtime selection concerns virtual function calls, not creation of the inheritance relationship. The supplied key B should not be memorized as a rule.
A1-019: A new expression creates an object during program execution and normally requests dynamic storage. Car* p = new Car; stores a pointer, not the whole object, in p. Pair owning raw new with the matching delete, or prefer a smart pointer in practical C++.
A1-020: The key uses the older textbook rule that constructors and destructors are not inherited like ordinary methods. Since C++11, using Base::Base can inherit constructors, while destructors are not inherited. Without a language-version assumption the alternatives do not express one stable modern answer.
A1-021: Single, multiple, multilevel, hierarchical and hybrid are common teaching names for inheritance shapes. 'Distributed inheritance' is not one of these standard introductory categories. Draw the parent/child arrows to distinguish multiple from multilevel.
A1-022: Compilation translates or prepares a program for execution. It is not an OOP pillar. Inheritance and polymorphism describe how programs organize related types and behavior, whether the language is compiled or interpreted.
A1-023: Multiple inheritance means one derived class has more than one direct base: class C : public A, public B. Multilevel means a chain, A -> B -> C. Here D literally says 'Multiple inheritance'; it is not the usual multiple-true option.
A1-024: Alan Kay is associated with naming and developing the object-oriented approach in Smalltalk, so C is the intended option. Earlier object-oriented class concepts came from Simula, developed by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. Do not interpret the answer as saying that Kay alone invented every OOP concept.
A1-025: A virtual function enables runtime dispatch through a suitable base pointer or reference. If that reference denotes a Car, its overridden start() can run even when the reference type is Vehicle. Ordinary overloading is selected at compile time instead.
A1-026: Reusing well-tested components can reduce repeated testing work and maintenance effort, so B and C motivate D. Reuse does not guarantee faster compilation, and reused code still needs integration tests. Treat these as possible engineering benefits, not mathematical guarantees.
A1-027: A C++ constructor cannot have the trailing const qualifier used on member functions. It must initialize the new object. You can still construct a const Car object; that is different from declaring Car() const.
A1-028: A C++ class template describes a family of classes parameterized by types or values. For example, Box<int> and Box<double> come from template<class T> class Box. Java generics look similar but have different language rules and implementation behavior.
A1-029: C++ struct members are public unless an access label changes that. C++ class members are private by default. Both can have methods, constructors, inheritance and access labels; struct is not restricted to data only in C++.
A1-030: Default, parameterized and copy constructors are recognized introductory categories. 'Friend constructor' is not a separate constructor category. A constructor of another class can be granted friendship, but that does not create a new special-member category.
A1-031: An abstract class cannot be directly instantiated. A parent class is not necessarily abstract, and unnamed class objects can be declared in C++. Look for pure virtual functions in C++ rather than assuming every base class is abstract.
A1-032: All three listed operators, ||, << and &&, can be overloaded for suitable user-defined types, so D replaces the supplied key B. Overloaded logical operators do not preserve the built-in short-circuit evaluation guarantee. The fact that << is common for stream output does not make it the only overloadable operator.
A1-033: Function overloading is both ad-hoc polymorphism and compile-time polymorphism in the usual terminology. A and C therefore overlap, making D appropriate under this assignment's multiple-true convention. It is not the runtime selection associated with virtual functions.
A1-034: The usual friend function declared by a class is not a member of that class. Friendship grants access; it does not attach an implicit this pointer. Static and virtual member functions, by contrast, are class members.
A1-035: Overriding supplies a derived implementation of an inherited virtual operation in C++. That supports polymorphism: one base interface, different runtime behavior. Merely declaring another non-virtual function with the same name is not sufficient for virtual dispatch.
A1-036: Use delete on a pointer obtained by a matching single-object new expression. It invokes the destructor and releases the storage. free belongs with malloc/calloc and must not be used as a replacement for delete on a normal new-created C++ object.
A1-037: Late binding is the runtime choice of an override, normally through a virtual member function. A static member function has no current object on which to base virtual dispatch. Friendship and inlining concern other language features.
A1-038: Non-member operators such as + and binary * can be friends, so more than one listed option is possible. In C++17, assignment operator= must be a non-static member, not a non-member friend overload. Friend is needed only when that function requires privileged access.
A1-039: The question says 'passed as a function', but the key explains passing an object as an argument. Objects can be passed by value, pointer or reference; callable objects can also define operator(). Because these are different ideas, the printed wording is retained for review without scoring it.
A1-040: Ad-hoc polymorphism is the usual name associated with function overloading. Several functions share a name but handle different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the applicable overload; virtual polymorphism is a different mechanism.
A1-041: In a C++ class, members are private until an access label says otherwise. This answer assumes the surrounding C++ context. In a C++ struct the default is public; in Java an unmodified member normally has package access; Python uses different conventions.
A1-042: Both malloc and calloc allocate dynamic raw storage, so A, B and their summary C are true and D follows the paper's convention. calloc zeroes the allocated bytes; malloc does not. Neither calls a C++ object's constructor.
A1-043: Encapsulation binds state and operations into a unit and controls access. Abstraction hides unnecessary implementation detail behind a useful interface. The short answer 'binding and hiding' is a memory aid, not a claim that encapsulation and abstraction never overlap.
A1-044: Among these options, class is the mechanism used to implement an abstract data type with a controlled interface. int and double are built-in scalar types. Strictly, a class is not automatically a well-designed ADT; behavior and interface contracts matter too.
A1-045: Message passing means asking another object to perform an operation, commonly by calling its method. For example, account.deposit(100) sends a request to an account object. It need not mean a network message or a special messaging service.
A1-046: Encapsulation can support abstraction: private implementation details stay behind public operations. Users can call deposit() without knowing the internal representation. Polymorphism and inheritance require additional mechanisms and are not automatic consequences of encapsulation.
A1-047: There is no general OOP rule that inheritance reduces the need for nested classes. Nesting and inheritance solve different design problems. The key chooses B, but the question gives no concrete design in which that claim can be tested.
A1-048: 'Friend constructor' is not a standard introductory constructor category. Default constructors allow a zero-argument call; parameterized constructors accept supplied arguments. Friendship is an access relationship, not a construction category.
A1-049: Neither ?: nor the built-in member-access dot . can be overloaded in C++. The stream extraction operator >> can be overloaded for suitable user-defined types. Therefore A and B make D the intended choice.
A1-050: Constructors cannot be virtual. Destructors can be virtual, and ordinary non-static member functions can be virtual. The constructor establishes the object; virtual dispatch is not a way to select which constructor to run.
A1-051: An object has identity, state (attributes) and behavior. A source-code variable name is not essential: an object can exist without a named variable referring to it. Two names may also refer to the same object, as you have seen with Python lists.
A1-052: None of the listed pairs are the same concept, so E corrects the supplied D. Encapsulation controls the unit and access; abstraction exposes only relevant detail; inheritance creates a type relationship; polymorphism allows different implementations behind an interface. Related is not identical.
A1-053: You do not need an input/output header merely to define a class or use inheritance. Language features are not enabled by #include <iostream>. Include headers only for the library facilities you use; the old iostream.h spelling is non-standard in modern C++.
A1-054: 'Always increases overhead' is false. Overloaded calls can be resolved at compile time, and optimizers can simplify even virtual calls in suitable circumstances. Polymorphism can improve readability and flexibility, but those benefits also depend on design.
A1-055: Static member functions can be overloaded, so they can participate in compile-time polymorphism. Constructor overloading and member-function overloading are also valid examples. E corrects a key that appears to confuse all polymorphism with runtime virtual dispatch.
A1-056: In the intended runtime-polymorphism context, a virtual function is the characteristic mechanism. An arbitrary class member or inline function need not be polymorphic. Note that this is an example of polymorphism, not an exhaustive definition of every kind.
A1-057: Overload resolution chooses the viable function that best matches the arguments under the language rules. It does not automatically choose a global function or a local function first. Ties or no suitable candidate produce an error; an abstract class does not introduce a separate call-priority rule.
A1-058: In older exam terminology, an 'object-based' language has objects but lacks the full inheritance/polymorphism model assumed by that textbook. These labels are not a universal modern language taxonomy. In particular, JavaScript supports prototype-based inheritance and must not be described simply as having no polymorphism.
A1-059: A C++ class may have no member functions at all, and a C++ program need not use classes. Thus the mandatory claims A and C are false, making D the multiple-false answer. C++ supports procedural as well as object-oriented programming.
A1-060: The key A is meaningful only when comparing a C++ class with a C struct. In C++, structs can have member functions, constructors and access control too. If both types are C++, no option describes the actual default-access distinction; the language context is missing.
A1-061: Dynamic binding is another name for runtime or late binding. It is about selecting the implementation of an operation. Dynamic typing concerns when types are checked, and dynamic loading concerns bringing code into a running program; neither is the same thing.
A1-062: A non-member friend function is granted access without becoming a member. A virtual member, a const-qualified member and a static member are still members. Here D literally means friend function, so read the full option rather than assuming D always means multiple answers.
A1-063: A non-member friend may overload binary *. In C++17, operator() and operator-> must be non-static member functions, so they cannot be implemented as non-member friend overloads. This question uses the C++17 baseline stated for this pack.
A1-064: Encapsulation groups state with the operations responsible for it and limits direct access. 'Secure' here means controlled program access, not encryption or a defense against every attack. Think of a validated deposit() operation rather than unrestricted balance changes.
A1-065: The ordinary teaching rule is that a derived class cannot directly access a base's private members. However, a base can explicitly grant friendship to that derived class. Since the question says 'never' without excluding friendship, key C is too absolute; distinguish normal inheritance access from granted friendship.
A1-066: C++ class types do have sizeof values, so the key's C is wrong. Object layout includes non-static member subobjects, base subobjects, alignment and possibly implementation overhead; it is not simply the largest member or an unqualified sum. Static members are separate, and even an empty complete class object has nonzero size.
A1-067: A parent, nested or unnamed class can have an object, provided its own definition permits it. None of the listed categories is inherently non-instantiable. An abstract class would be the usual answer, but that category is not listed.
A1-068: Unrestricted global mutable state can weaken encapsulation, which is why the key chooses C. But a global variable does not automatically violate every encapsulation rule: internal-linkage implementation state is a counterexample. The question needs a particular access/design context before 'violates' becomes a strict fact.
A1-069: The intended definition groups data and the operations that work on that data into one unit. It is not merely a collection of functions or merely a collection of variables. There need not literally be 'more than one' of each for encapsulation to be useful.
A1-070: A, B and C each provide a complete, legal object declaration in this setting. D declares an actual array s with neither a bound nor an initializer, so its size cannot be determined. This is different from an extern declaration of an incomplete array.
A1-071: C++ puts the keyword before the class name: class student { ... };. A reverses that order. B's private constructor may prevent outside construction, but a private constructor is not itself a syntax error.
A1-072: Objects can be passed by value, pointer or reference, and callable class objects can be used in function-like contexts. 'Passed as function' has no precise meaning here and also conflicts with question 39's wording. Preserve the key B as source material, but do not derive a general language rule from it.
A1-073: Platform independence is an execution/deployment property, not a necessary OOP concept. C++ supports OOP even though its usual compiled binaries are platform-specific. Message passing and data hiding are common object-oriented ideas.
A1-074: C++ does not require every program to use classes or objects of user-defined classes. Encapsulation can also be organized through modules and controlled interfaces outside class syntax. The options conflate a particular class-based design with a universal programming requirement, so the key D is not a reliable scored rule.
A1-075: Message passing means one object requests behavior from another, such as order.calculateTotal(). In ordinary class-based examples this is a method call. It is not necessarily a raw transfer of fields or a network protocol.
A1-076: Abstraction hides implementation details while exposing relevant information and operations. Thus B and C express the intended pair and support D. It does not mean hiding the important interface that the user actually needs.
A1-077: The source key B intends a class as the unit combining data and code. However, the phrase 'combination of abstraction of the data and code' does not distinguish a class definition from an object or an interface clearly enough. Learn the separate definitions rather than memorizing this vague sentence.
A1-078: Abstraction can support OOP and can help avoid duplication, but neither statement is a unique definition. 'Use abstraction at its minimum' is not a language rule. The source's B is retained for comparison, while the printed question remains unscored.
A1-079: The intended benefit is representation independence: private internals may change without changing clients if the public contract remains compatible. 'Without modifying any other code' is not guaranteed, and methods do not change a field's declared type at runtime. Key C needs those missing assumptions.
A1-080: Encapsulation can protect invariants to some extent by restricting ordinary access. It does not guarantee complete security: an unsafe interface can still expose or corrupt state. The qualified answer A is therefore better than the absolute claim B.
A1-081: Returning a writable pointer to private state lets callers bypass controlled operations, so A describes the design risk and B can also be true. The program itself is syntactically valid; merely taking the uninitialized member's address is not reading its value. Because more than one substantive option is defensible and no combined option is supplied, this item is not scored.
A1-082: For a C++ class, an omitted access label means private. For a struct, it means public. Remember that this rule applies to both data members and member functions until another access label appears.
A1-083: If Car declares friend class Inspector, Inspector's members may access Car's private and protected members. The permission is granted by Car, not claimed by Inspector. Friendship is not automatically reciprocal, transitive or inherited.
A1-084: Polymorphism means one operation or interface can work in different forms. A base reference may invoke different overrides depending on the actual object. Overloading is a separate compile-time example of the same broad 'many forms' idea.
A1-085: student_details supplies the pure virtual operation, while topper and average supply different implementations. Together they form the polymorphic hierarchy. The declarations alone are not a complete runnable program, but they do not need an unrelated failed class to express that design.
A1-086: A small function is the usual candidate when the goal is to remove call overhead. The optimizer decides whether machine-code inlining actually happens; the inline keyword is not a promise. In C++, inline also has important multiple-definition/linkage rules beyond this performance mnemonic.
A1-087: There are three variables named x, but ::x explicitly selects the global one. Its value is 1. The local values 2 and 3 would matter only if the expression referred to those scopes instead.
A1-088: A private destructor can prevent ordinary outside automatic destruction, and a factory/friend can control creation and deletion. A private constructor alone restricts who constructs, not whether that trusted code uses stack or dynamic storage. The key's blanket 'B and C' rule is not sufficient to enforce heap-only allocation in every context.
A1-089: Both vector objects are dynamically allocated and never deleted in the program. Moreover, each vector is empty, so it contains no a objects whose destructor could print. A pointer going out of scope does not automatically delete its pointee, and a vector of raw pointers would not own/delete those pointees by itself.
A1-090: The global array has static storage duration and is zero-initialized before main. Therefore x[99] is 0. Do not transfer this rule to an uninitialized automatic local int array, whose elements do not receive this same initialization.
A1-091: A member function generally has access privileges for its class, so A captures the intended rule. C is also included in that access, while B's wording treats functions as per-object entities. 'Always' also overlooks the object needed to use a non-static field. The alternatives do not support one exclusive answer.
A1-092: Both A and B are false: virtual functions need not be public and cannot be static. A base pointer is one way to perform dynamic dispatch, but a base reference works as well. The multiple-false choice D is the intended answer.
A1-093: This question fails to say runtime polymorphism. Compile-time polymorphism through overloading needs neither inheritance nor virtual functions. Even for runtime dispatch, a pointer can be used instead of a reference. The key D should not be learned as an unconditional requirement for all C++ polymorphism.
A1-094: In Java, final appears before the method's return type; in C++, it appears after the member-function declarator, as void f() final. The surrounding questions are C++, but the supplied key B describes Java-style placement. Because the language is not specified, this item is retained without scoring.
A1-095: Overloading supports compile-time polymorphism: one function name can accept different parameter lists. Default arguments let some arguments be omitted; they do not themselves create a new overload. Inheritance and encapsulation are different concepts.
A1-096: None of the four changes creates a distinct overload signature in the illustrated forms. Return type alone cannot overload; array parameters adjust to pointers; adding a default argument is a redeclaration, not a new overload. Mixing static and non-static-linkage declarations also needs context. The key D even says 'all except 2 and 4', text that does not match printed option D, so this item is deliberately unscored.
A1-097: The declaration gives both parameters a default of 0. fun(5) supplies x = 5 and uses y = 0, so x + y is 5. Defaults are used at the call site even though the later function definition does not repeat them.
A1-098: t1 is non-const, so overload resolution selects fun(); t2 is const, so it selects fun() const. The output is fun() followed by fun() const, with the printed line breaks. The source answer is mislabeled 99 rather than 98; no separate question 99 is printed.
A1-100: A and B are both incorrect: virtual functions can be non-public and cannot be static. The paper supplies no combined 'more than one' choice here, so key B alone is not unique. Calling through a reference also works, and a pure virtual declaration need not have an ordinary base definition.
A2-001: In the ordinary C++17 member-function model, this identifies the current object during a non-static member call. It is often explained as an implicit object argument. Static member functions have no current object and no this pointer; an optimizing compiler need not literally pass a physical pointer in every machine-code call.
A2-002: The program fails to compile because fun2 is static and tries to use this. Static functions can call other static functions as fun1() or Test::fun1(), but this->fun1() requires a this pointer that does not exist. Since no printed option says compilation error, select E, not one of the proposed outputs.
A2-003: obj has automatic storage, not storage obtained by new. delete this therefore attempts an invalid deallocation; accessing the object afterward introduces another lifetime problem. This is undefined behavior, not a guaranteed print of x = 0 and not necessarily a compiler error. Do not execute it to infer a portable answer.
A2-004: Each complete object has its own non-static data-member subobjects. Static data is shared for the class, while method code is not conceptually copied into every object. Thus saying every object shares all fields or owns a separate copy of all method code is misleading.
A2-005: Use the question's stated model, not your machine's sizeof values. ptr contributes 4 bytes and y contributes 4; static x is stored separately. With no padding, sizeof(t) is 8 and the separately stated pointer size is 4, producing 8 4.
A2-006: A header file is source included during preprocessing, not a runtime argument value. Constants and structure objects can be arguments. An array argument usually adjusts to a pointer parameter in the illustrated C/C++ function-call model; passing it is not the same as copying its entire contents.
A2-007: The intended key is overrides, which describes an eligible Java instance method or a C++ override of a virtual base member. In C++, a same-name, same-signature non-virtual member can instead hide the base member. Because the language and virtual requirement are omitted, this item is discussion-only.
A2-008: A non-member friend has access to the granting class's private and protected members without becoming a member of that class. Its friend declaration may appear in any access section. Friendship is a specific permission, not a requirement to put the function in private.
A2-009: b has static type Base* but points to a Derived object. Because show is virtual, b->show() dispatches to Derived::show and prints Derived. The example leaks its allocation; that does not change this printed call, but practical code should manage ownership safely.
A2-010: Encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism are all object-oriented concepts. No listed substantive option is the requested non-feature, so E is correct. Compilation and platform independence would be examples of different categories, but they are not offered here.
A2-011: Overloading provides the same function name with distinct parameter lists. Return type alone cannot distinguish two overloads in C++ or Java. The compiler must be able to choose based on the call's arguments, not on a vague claim that one function has several purposes.
A2-012: Scope resolution :: cannot be overloaded in C++. +, = and [] can be overloaded subject to their language restrictions. Operator overloading customizes operations involving user-defined types; it cannot create new tokens or change operator precedence.
A2-013: In this pointer-owning context, a shallow copy copies the pointer value so both objects refer to the same allocation. A deep copy creates a separate allocation and copies the represented data. The exact depth is a design choice; plain assignment of a Java or Python reference is aliasing, not even an outer-object copy.
A2-014: The defining syntax is a virtual member declaration with = 0. A pure virtual member may still have an out-of-class definition, so A is not a universal rule. A derived class may remain abstract instead of overriding it, so B's unconditional 'must' is also false. C corrects the supplied D.
A2-015: For the C++17 baseline, a class has one destructor and it cannot be overloaded by arguments. Destructors may be virtual. An explicit call such as obj.~T() ends the lifetime but does not itself free the object's storage, so B is not a correct description of deallocation. Newer language versions have additional prospective-destructor rules, outside this baseline.
A2-016: A static member function has no implicit this, but it may access a non-static field through an explicit object, such as obj.x when access is permitted. Static methods can be overloaded, and ordinary instance methods may access static fields. Therefore C corrects the key E; 'cannot access directly without an object' is the rule to remember.
A2-017: Test::x starts at 0. The first getX prints 0; constructing the array t[5] calls the constructor five times and increments the same shared x to 5. The second getX prints 5, so the result is 0 5.
A2-018: After a parameter receives a default argument, subsequent ordinary parameters must also have defaults available. Here z has none after x and y do, so the declaration is invalid. The program does not produce 10, 0 or 20; E stands for the unlisted compilation error.
A2-019: Both pointer arguments refer to number. In the two-argument overload, one multiplication operand reads number while the other modifies it through --(*y), with no sequencing between those operands. That is undefined behavior in C++17, not a guaranteed 870. E corrects the key C; executing it and observing 870 would not establish a valid portable answer.
A2-020: The explicit assumptions say int = 4 bytes, pointer = 4 bytes and no alignment padding. Only ptr and y occupy the instance, so 4 + 4 = 8. Static x is separate; sizeof(Test*) is the assumed 4, giving 8 4. This duplicates question 5 and is intentionally retained.
A2-021: An abstract C++ class cannot be instantiated with or without new, so B and C are false. C++ also has no abstract class keyword: abstractness follows from a pure virtual final overrider. D is the intended multiple-incorrect choice; Java's abstract declaration rule must not be copied into C++.
A2-022: C++ supports nested classes, but the language does not define a universal count of 'two types of nested classes'. Static versus non-static nested/inner categories are commonly taught for Java, not as this C++ taxonomy. The key A is retained as a source claim, not a graded language fact.
A2-023: In Java, assigning an object-reference variable copies the reference, so both variables can denote the same object. Python name assignment similarly aliases the object. But assigning through C++ references usually assigns the referred-to object's value rather than reseating a reference. The omitted language makes source key B conditional.
A2-024: The shared next_id starts at 1. p1 stores 1 and increments it; p2 stores 2; p3 stores 3. Each object has its own id but all constructors use the same next_id, so the output is 1 2 3.
A2-025: fun was declared as a non-static member. An out-of-class definition cannot change it into a static member by adding static there. Declare static in the class declaration and omit it from the out-of-class definition; as printed, the program is a compilation error.
A2-026: fun increments the shared count, prints it, and returns *this by reference. That return value lets the next .fun() call operate on the same object. Four chained calls print 1 2 3 4; returning a new value or void would be a different design.
A2-027: The first getX sees the shared counter at 0. Five array elements are then constructed, adding five to that same counter. The second call sees 5. This is a repeated source question and has not been removed from the bank.
A2-028: Ordinary derived-class code cannot directly access a base's private members, regardless of whether inheritance is public, protected or private. Private inheritance changes accessibility of inherited public/protected interfaces; it does not turn the base's private data into accessible derived data. Explicit friendship would be a separate permission.
A2-029: R inherits from Q, and lookup finds Q::print before the hidden P::print. Therefore r.print() prints Inside Q. There is no ambiguous pair of direct bases here and no virtual dispatch is needed for this direct call.
A2-030: When d is destroyed, Derived's destructor body runs first. Direct base subobjects are then destroyed in reverse construction order: Base2 and then Base1. Read the base declaration list rather than the order in which the destructor definitions appear in the file.
A2-031: A pointer to an accessible unambiguous base can point to a derived object, so Base* bp = new Derived is valid. A freshly allocated Base object is not a Derived object, so it cannot initialize Derived* implicitly. The error is the second pointer initialization.
A2-032: *q = "abcde" changes p to that string. ++p advances to b and s remembers that position. Reassigning p to another string does not move s. ++s advances from b to c, and dereferencing it prints c; const protects the characters, not these pointer variables.
A2-033: Const-qualified non-static members, const parameters, and static const data members are all possible. A reference itself cannot be cv-qualified like a separate object, but a reference can refer to const data. The numbered combination choices and option D do not clearly encode these distinctions, so the supplied D is not scored.
A2-034: The assignment x = 10 attempts to modify a const int, so the program is rejected. Under C++ the uninitialized const declaration is already an error; under C that declaration has different initialization rules, but the later assignment still violates const. Either way, there is no valid output of 10.
A2-035: int const and const int express the same const-qualified integer type. s is initialized to 9, and reading a const variable is allowed. Only later modification would be prohibited, so the program prints 9.
A2-036: These describe the ordinary virtual-call model: eligible derived members override, virtual calls enable runtime polymorphism, and the actual object determines the final overrider.
